column4: The section names the root ب ن ي for building palaces and places Thamud's palaces in the plains beside mountain-carved homes. This verse gives both forms of settlement that the leveling of the people reverses.
The section links carved dwellings to a people who thought they were secure; this verse says they carved mountain homes while آمنين, making the collapse of built refuge concrete.
The section's mountain-house image is stated again of Thamud here: they carve dwellings in the mountains, so the later flattening reaches a people who made homes in rock.
The section cites the root ط ح و for flat terrain and the rock-cut Thamud. This verse identifies Thamud as those who cut rock in the valley, joining the people to the landform later leveled.
The section's root ع ق ر is the camel-hamstringing that precedes the people's leveling; this verse says they hamstrung the she-camel, supplying that precise deed in its narrative context.
The section names ع ق ر for the camel's hamstringing before the people are struck down. This verse narrates that same act and its three-day warning.
This verse says Thamud hamstrung the she-camel, the exact deed named through the section's root ع ق ر before their destruction.
The section's root ع ق ر names the decisive blow against the camel; this verse states that the people hamstrung her, immediately before the punishment arrives.
The section describes the people leveled after building on the plain; this verse leaves Thamud جاثمين in their homes, giving the bodily result of that leveling.
This verse likewise leaves Thamud in their homes after the blast. Its fallen-in-place scene makes the section's account of the community being laid flat tangible.
The section says Thamud's settlement is erased by the leveling; this verse says their homes look as though they had never lived there, showing what remains after the people are gone.
The section moves from Thamud's elevated and carved homes to their destruction; this verse calls their houses خَاوِيَةً because of their wrongdoing, showing the settlement emptied and collapsed.
The section cites the image of Thamud becoming dry crushed plant matter; this verse says they became هَشِيمِ الْمُحْتَظِرِ, carrying the same specific dry-stalk aftermath.
The section names Thamud's inability to rise after the punishment. This verse states that they could not manage قيام, the bodily opposite of the formed and standing human.
The section's flattened people are set against the spread ground; here the mountains are removed and the land is left قَاعًا صَفْصَفًا, making a level surface the scene of judgment.
This continuation specifies that the leveled land has no عِوَجًا وَلَا أَمْتًا, an exact contourless landscape for the section's image of leveling.
The section treats the spread earth as the prior form of leveling; this verse asks how the earth was سُطِحَتْ, directly presenting its spread, even surface.

The section pairs God's shaping of the soul with the leveling of Thamud as acts of one power. This verse says He can نُسَوِّيَ بنانه, restore even the fingertips, making the small-scale shaping an explicit counterpart to destruction.

The section's named root س و ي first describes a soul formed in proportion. This verse uses فَسَوَّىٰكَ for God's proportioning of the human being, grounding the same shaping action elsewhere in the Quran.
After saying God formed the human, this verse says He assembled him in whichever image He willed. It extends the section's formed-human side of the contrast with Thamud being laid flat.
The section connects سَوَّى to bringing a being into due form; this verse uses فَسَوَّىٰ in the same divine act of creation and proportioning.
The section compares the destroyed Thamud to dry plant debris; this verse uses هَشِيمًا for vegetation reduced to dry fragments, while its parable shows how quickly a flourishing scene disappears.
The section's spread ground is later made level; this verse says the earth is extended, مُدَّتْ, at the end, turning the same ground into an eschatological scene.

Following the earth's extension in 84:3, this verse says it casts out what is within it and becomes empty. That completes the section's image of a surface left after the people and their dwellings are gone.
After the secure mountain homes in 15:82, this verse says the cry seized their people at daybreak. It supplies the destruction that reverses the security described in the linked verse.
After the hamstringing in 26:157, this verse says the punishment seized them. It completes the section's sequence from the camel's injury to the community's leveling.
The section includes بَنَىٰهَا and the lexicon's building sense; this verse says God built the heaven, setting divine construction alongside the human palaces whose builders are later leveled.
The section's named root ب ن ي is used here of God's building the heaven. That gives the human construction in the section a direct Quranic counterpart under the same root.
After the heaven is built in the same passage, this verse says the earth was spread. It recalls the section's spread ground as the setting on which human structures rise and can be leveled.
The section's image begins from the earth spread out before the people are laid flat; this verse describes the earth as spread, making the habitable ground itself part of the parallel.
This verse describes the earth as spread and then names its provisions. It recalls the section's plain as a prepared human dwelling-place before Thamud's settlement is erased.
The section treats the spread earth as the prior surface of the leveling; this verse says the earth was spread and set firm, a direct counterpart to the later contourless plain.
This verse again describes the earth as spread with mountains set upon it. It supplies the created terrain against which the section's mountain-cut homes and final leveling are read.

The section's root ب ن ي links building to the human palaces, while this verse places a built canopy over an earth made as a bed. Together they frame the human construction as something raised on God's prepared ground.
This verse calls the earth a cradle and lays paths through it. It makes the section's stretched ground a provision for dwelling before human settlements are leveled.
This verse also describes the earth as a cradle with paths. It gives a habitable, prepared surface as the prior condition to the section's flattened settlement.
The section reads the spread earth as the surface later leveled; this verse says God made the earth a بساط, a laid-out expanse for people.
By calling the earth a مهاد, this verse presents the ground as a laid-out habitation, the stable surface that the section shows becoming an even plain.

The verse between heaven's construction and earth's spreading describes the heaven as raised and proportioned; it continues the section's linked images of divine building, shaping, and the ground below.
This verse says mountains were set in the earth lest it sway with people. The section shows mountain homes and then a leveling that removes the terrain, a reversal of this stabilizing role.
This verse says the mountains are set moving and the earth made exposed. It extends the section's mountain-to-level-land image into the judgment scene.

The question about the mountains introduces the removal that leaves a plain in 20:106–107. Its own contribution is to make the mountains, also the place of Thamud's homes, the thing removed before leveling.

The section names the root س و ي for leveling people; this verse uses تُسَوَّىٰ for the disbelievers' wish that the earth be leveled over them. It turns the section's imposed destruction into the condemned people's own wish.
Before Thamud hamstrings the camel, Saleh presents her as a sign and forbids harming her. This warning sets the precise act in the section against a stated boundary.
Saleh commands his people to leave God's camel grazing in God's earth and not harm her. This is the explicit boundary that their hamstringing in 11:65 and the section's destruction cross.
In the passage leading to the hamstringing, this verse assigns the she-camel a drinking turn. It completes the camel scene behind the section's mention of her injury.
This verse warns Thamud not to touch the she-camel with harm after her assigned drink. It states the boundary violated in the next verse's hamstringing.
This verse presents the she-camel as a trial for Thamud just before the water-sharing instruction and hamstringing. It supplies the test that makes the section's named act culpable.
The camel's water is divided between her and the people before they hamstring her in 54:29. This verse gives the specific shared resource and boundary behind the section's act.

Like Thamud in 7:78, the deniers of Shuʿayb end جاثمين in their homes after an earthquake. The repeated bodily and domestic aftermath clarifies that the section's laying-flat scene is a Quranic judgment pattern.
This verse says Shuʿayb's deniers seem never to have lived there, echoing the disappearance stated of Thamud in 11:68 and making the emptied settlement a repeated aftermath.
This verse applies the same “as though they had never lived there” aftermath to Madyan that 11:68 gives for Thamud; it sharpens the section's image of a people erased from their settlement.
The people of Madyan are seized by the earthquake and left in their homes, paralleling Thamud's prostrate bodies in the section and its cited 7:78.

This verse pictures flourishing vegetation becoming harvested as though it had not flourished the previous day. It parallels the section's dry-stalk aftermath and Thamud's homes seeming never inhabited.
This verse's worldly-life crop yellows and becomes debris. It connects the section's dry remains to a Quranic image of what flourishes only to be brought down.

The question immediately before the fingertip verse asks whether human bones can be gathered. It supplies the resurrection problem to which 75:4 answers by asserting God's power even over the fingertips.
The denier asks who can revive bones after decay; this is the destruction-and-restoration question that 36:79 answers and that the section's shaped fingertip invokes.
This verse answers that God revives the bones by recalling their first creation. It links the section's fine divine shaping to God's power after bodily ruin.
This verse says God created people, made their forms good, and to Him is the return. It joins the section's formed-human image to the return after the leveling of a people.
This verse says the human was created in the best stature, a nonlexical parallel to the section's balanced, formed soul before its contrasting account of people laid flat.
After the best stature in 95:4, this verse describes the descent to the lowest state. It gives a specific form-to-lowering reversal like the section's passage from proportioning to leveling.
The section leaves Thamud unable to rise; here the earth splits open and the dead hurry out to their Lord. The contrast shows the final rising that follows the prostrate state.
Where the section says the punished people could not rise, this verse has the dead rise from graves and hasten to their Lord, making resurrection the pointed reversal of their fallen posture.

The section cites Thamud's rock-cut valley in 89:9; later in the same surah the earth is دُكَّتْ دَكًّا, pounded flat. The same landscape of human carving is answered by the ground itself being leveled.
